Glad Construction

GeometryConstructionsFractions
Game: See how a few straight lines can mark off exactly one Nth of the bottom side of a slanted box.
How to play: Drag the four corners to reshape the box, press − or + to choose the number of parts, and tick Show names to label the crossings.
3 parts
Look for the math

There is no measuring here. A line from one corner of a parallelogram to a mark on the opposite side meets the diagonal at a very predictable fraction. Repeat the step and you can cut off exactly one Nth of a side.

One crossing, one fraction

Start at the midpoint of the bottom side AB. The other diagonal DB crosses the diagonal AC in the middle, so its intersection E₀ is at 1/2 of AC. Drop a line from E₀ in the direction of the right side BC until it reaches AB: it lands at P₀, the midpoint of AB. The article's lemma says that if n·AP = AD, and Q is where BP meets AC, then

(n + 1)·AQ = AC

The proof uses similar triangles: since BC has the same length as AD, the triangles on either side of Q give QC/AQ = BC/AP = n, so AC/AQ = n + 1. For n = 1 this is the midpoint we started with.

Repeat the same step

Now draw the line from D to that midpoint P₀. It crosses AC at E₁, one third of the way along. The line through E₁ parallel to BC reaches AB at P₁, one third of the way along AB. The next line from D to P₁ gives 1/4, and so on. In general, for every k from 0 to N − 2,

AEₖ / AC = APₖ / AB = 1 / (k + 2)

This is the corollary on the article: the intercept theorem carries the same fraction from the diagonal down to the side. The logic test checks the formula for every N the applet allows, 2 to 20, over many different parallelograms, and compares each point with a second reading of the applet's own line-intersection code.

What this applet draws

The last mark P is at 1/N of AB, so the construction gives N equal parts. Drag the corners and the fractions do not change: only the shape of the box changes. The page also describes a variation that alternates which side holds the previous mark and produces the Fibonacci sequence of fractions; this applet always uses corner D, so its marks are 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, …, 1/N. The live cut-the-knot page no longer runs the Java applet — it shows a notice asking for Sun's Java VM — so the page's Explanation and the original class files were used to check the rules.

Try N = 2, then press + up to 20: watch the last green mark walk towards A while the diagonal crossings stay at the very same fractions.
